***

The coastline recedes beyond the very margins of our chart as we navigate a vast, open expanse of deep blue. Under high winds, our bow plows forcefully through the heavy swells of the ocean plain, leaving a boiling, salty fervor in our wake that dissipates within minutes—leaving only seabirds resting upon our bobbing crates, a thousand miles from land. To pass the time, I attempt to teach our boatswain’s mate "Sailing to Byzantium." Good-natured as he is, he responds only with endless laughter. 

It is by no means sufficient for a naval officer merely to be a capable mariner. He must be that, of course, but also so much more. He should embody the very soul of tact, patience, justice, firmness, and charity. No meritorious act by a subordinate should pass without reward, even if that reward is merely a word of approval. Conversely, he must not turn a blind eye to a single fault in those under his command. Yet, at the same time, he must be swift and unfailing in distinguishing honest error from malice, thoughtlessness from incompetence, and a well-intentioned shortcoming from a heedless or foolish blunder.

To occupy the time, I attempt to teach the boatswain’s mate the poem "Sailing to Byzantium," an effort he meets with continuous, good-natured laughter.

Being a skilled seafarer is far from the only requirement for a naval officer. Deep into the open ocean, the ship presses forward, navigating lonely waters more than a thousand miles from the nearest shore. In this vast, blue expanse, where the horizon offers neither variation nor relief, the rhythms of life aboard ship slow to a measured pulse, and the days can stretch endlessly ahead. 

To pass the time during these long stretches at sea, the narrator seeks out intellectual diversion, attempting to teach W.B. Yeats’s poem "Sailing to Byzantium" to a good-natured boatswain’s mate. This quiet exchange between poetry and practical seamanship serves as a reminder of the complex human dynamics that exist within the confines of a vessel. It highlights how life at sea demands a connection that bridges different backgrounds, intellects, and roles.

Reflecting on such interactions reveals a deeper truth about the nature of command: a naval officer must possess personal virtues that extend far beyond basic seamanship and technical skills. Navigational expertise and operational competence are merely the baseline. True leadership on the high seas requires a refined moral compass capable of guiding a crew through both routine monotony and sudden crisis.

Indeed, an ideal naval leader should embody a delicate balance of qualities, including tact, patience, justice, firmness, and charity. Tact allows an officer to manage interpersonal friction in close quarters, while patience ensures sound decision-making under stress. Justice and firmness provide the bedrock of discipline and trust, while charity ensures that authority is tempered with empathy and genuine concern for the welfare of the crew.

Ultimately, effective officers must exercise sharp discernment in their governance. They must be quick to acknowledge and praise the good acts of their subordinates, fostering a culture of pride and achievement. Equally important, however, is the ability to carefully distinguish between honest mistakes—born of enthusiasm or extreme conditions—and behavior rooted in genuine malice or incompetence. By blending technical mastery with moral clarity, a great officer earns not just obedience, but true respect, holding the ship and its crew steadfast no matter how far they sail from land.
outputs.L4:
The Atlantic had flattened into a expanse of slate-grey glass, stretching unbroken from horizon to horizon under the oppressive weight of a doldrum sky. For three weeks, the three-masted frigate *HMS Reliance* had made barely twenty leagues, her sails hanging limply from the yards like damp linen. On such a voyage, where time ceased to be measured by progress and instead by the agonizingly slow drip of the glass, a commander’s greatest enemy was not the sea, but the rot of idle spirits.

In the quiet sanctuary of the Great Cabin, framed by stern windows that looked out upon the endless, empty wake, Captain Edward Vance sat across from Midshipman Thomas Penrose. Between them on the polished mahogany table lay two items: a brass sextant, gleaming and precise, and a worn, leather-bound volume of Shakespeare’s *Tragedies*.

Penrose was nineteen, earnest, and fiercely ambitious, but possessed of the rigid, brittle certainty common to young officers who had learned the world entirely from naval regulations and signal books. For the past hour, Vance had been guiding the young man through the fourth act of *Othello*, a task he had undertaken initially to stave off the mind-numbing boredom of the calm, but which had quickly evolved into a far more serious endeavor.

"Read the passage again, Mr. Penrose," Vance said quietly, resting his weathered hands on the table. "And tell me not what Cassio *did*, but why he did it."

Penrose adjusted his collar, looking down at the text with an expression of acute discomfort. "He drank beyond his measure, sir, while on watch. He lost his temper and drew his blade. Under the Articles of War, it is a clear breach of discipline. He deserved his ruin."

Vance sighed, a low sound that mingled with the faint creak of the ship’s timbers. "You speak like a court-martial clerk, Thomas. You see the offense, but you are blind to the man. Cassio was seduced by a false friend who knew his weakness. His crime was not malice, nor was it treason. It was frail human stupidity, weaponized against him by a mind that was truly evil. Can you not see the difference between a man who stumbles in the dark and one who digs a pit for his brother?"

Penrose shifted, his brow furrowing. "A breach of duty is a breach of duty, Captain. If we excuse the stumble, the ship falls into chaos."

Vance leaned back, looking at the young officer with a mix of affection and grave concern. He saw in Penrose the raw material of a fine mariner—he could calculate a lunar distance with astonishing speed and knew every rope and stay in the ship’s rigging. Yet, as Vance well knew, technical seamanship was merely the mechanical skeleton of command. The soul of it lay elsewhere.

Earlier that morning, Penrose had recommended the flogging of an aging topman who had dropped a marlinspike from the mainmast, nearly striking a deckhand. Penrose had logged it as "gross negligence bordering on mutinous disregard." Vance had investigated quietly and discovered the old sailor’s sight was failing—a condition the man had desperately hidden for fear of being cast ashore to starve. The error was born of terror and physical decline, not malice. Penrose had wanted to break the man's skin; Vance had assigned him to the sail-locker to sew canvas, preserving both discipline and the old man’s dignity.

"Consider the sea, Mr. Penrose," Vance said, gesturing toward the stern windows. "Any fool can learn to trim a sail or steer a compass course when the wind is fair. That is mere seamanship. But command—true command—is the art of governing men. And men are not made of timber and iron. They are fragile, flawed creatures driven by fear, pride, ignorance, and devotion."

He stood up and walked to the window, watching the slow rise and fall of the swell. 

"A captain who governs solely by the letter of the law is not a leader; he is merely an executioner with a commission. To hold absolute power over two hundred souls aboard a wooden box in the middle of a vast ocean requires an extraordinary moral burden. It demands infinite patience. It requires you to look beneath the surface of a man’s failure."

Vance turned back to face the young man. "If a seaman commits a fault, your first duty is not to punish, but to discern. Was it born of defiance? Or was it the result of exhaustion, grief, or sheer ignorance? If it is malice, you must strike it down without hesitation, for it is a contagion. But if it is an innocent error—a human weakness—you must correct it with justice tempered by compassion. If you punish an innocent mistake with the severity due to treason, you do not instill discipline. You instill hatred. You break the man's spirit, and in doing so, you weaken the ship."

Penrose looked down at the book, his black-and-white world suddenly complicated by shades of grey he had never been taught to see. "And if one misjudges, sir? If one mistakes malice for innocence?"

"Then you have erred on the side of humanity," Vance replied softly. "Which is a far lighter weight to carry on your conscience than knowing you shattered an honest man out of pride or haste. Moral virtue is not a softness, Mr. Penrose. It is the highest form of strength. It is what separates a true commander from a tyrant."

Silence settled over the cabin, heavy and contemplative. Outside, a gentle breeze suddenly rustled the canvas overhead; the ship shuddered slightly as the sails caught the light air, and the slow, rhythmic lap of water against the hull resumed.

Penrose looked up from the book, his eyes reflecting a newfound depth of understanding. "Shall I read the next scene, Captain?"

Vance smiled faintly, sitting back down. "Read on, Mr. Penrose. Let us see if we can teach you how to read the hearts of men before we reach port."
outputs.L5:
**The Invisible Conductor**

Before the journey begins, there is only stillness. The open water holds its breath, mirror-like and patient under a vast sky. But then comes the shift—a gentle ripple on the surface, a cool whisper across the deck, and a sudden tautness in the rigging. 

**Sailing** is, at its heart, an ancient dialogue between humanity and the elements. You cannot see **the wind**, but you can feel its weight, hear its song in the stay-wires, and watch it transform a piece of simple canvas into a surging engine of kinetic power. As the sail fills, the vessel awakens. It leans into the water with a quiet, confident grace, carving a bright white wake through the deep blue.

Unlike motorized travel, which forces its way across the landscape, a sailboat moves in partnership with the atmosphere. To master the craft is not to conquer nature, but to listen to it. The sailor must learn to read the unseen—watching for the darkening shadows of gusts on the water’s surface, sensing subtle shifts in temperature, and constantly adjusting the trim to capture the breeze's changing moods. 

In those moments when the hull glides effortlessly forward, propelled by nothing more than air and angle, the chaos of the world shore-side fades away. There is only the rhythmic rush of parting waves, the tension of the lines, and the quiet thrill of motion. 

Ultimately, **sailing** offers a timeless lesson in living: we may never be able to direct **the wind**, but by understanding its power, we can always set our course toward new horizons.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective journal entry from the perspective of a naval officer on a long ocean voyage. Include vivid descriptions of the sea, a lighthearted attempt to teach poetry to a subordinate, and a meditation on the qualities of a good leader based on historic naval doctrine.
counterfactuals.output:
**12th October, 1847**  
*HMS Sovereign, Forty Leagues off the Tristan da Cunha Group*  
*Position: 37°12' S, 12°20' W. Wind: West-South-West, fresh. Sea: Heavy swell.*

***

The glass has been steady all evening, though the sea tells a grander, wilder story than the barometer lets on. 

For forty days we have known nothing but the infinite blue desert. Today, the ocean was a masterclass in motion and light. At mid-day, the swell rose in great, muscular ridges of bruised cobalt, crowned with brilliant crests of spume that the wind tore away into fine white lace. To look over the taffrail is to gaze into a liquid abyss—an endless, rolling solitude that makes a man feel at once entirely insignificant and fiercely alive. By dusk, the water had softened to the color of molten lead, reflecting a sky stained with plum and cold rose. Now, in the middle watch, the darkness is absolute save for the churn of our wake, which burns with a pale, cold phosphorescence, as if the ship were plowing through a field of fallen stars. 

It is easy to become solemn in such a place, which is why I found myself seeking levity earlier today. 

During the afternoon dogwatch, I caught young Midshipman Hawkins slumped over the log-book in the chartroom, looking as thoroughly miserable as a boy forced to do arithmetic on a holiday. Upon inquiry, he admitted his uncle had insisted he "refine his mind" during the voyage by committing poetry to memory. The poor lad was hopelessly bogged down in Lord Byron’s *Childe Harold*.

"I simply do not grasp it, Lieutenant," Hawkins complained, rubbing his temples. "'Roll on, thou deep and dark blue Ocean—roll!' Why tell it to roll? It’s going to roll anyway, sir. It doesn't need his permission."

I could not help but laugh. I spent the next half-hour attempting to explain the nature of poetic metaphor to a boy whose entire world is measured in knots, fathoms, and rum rations. I tried to guide him through a stanza on the majesty of the wind, suggesting he feel the rhythm of the meter like the pitch of the deck underfoot. 

He stared at me, deadpan, and remarked, "With respect, sir, if Byron had to reef the topsails in a gale off Cape Horn, he’d have spent less time writing iambs and more time holding onto the rigging." 

I surrendered the lesson then, deciding the Navy had gained a fine future mariner, even if the literary world had lost a critic.

Yet, watching Hawkins return to his duties on the quarterdeck afterward, my thoughts turned to the heavier burdens that await him—and indeed, those that rest on my own shoulders. 

A ship of war is a small, wooden universe, adrift in an uncaring element. To govern it requires more than just knowing how to trim a sail or aim a carronade; it requires the art of command. I found myself thinking of Lord Nelson’s famous dictum: *“First, gain the affection of your officers and crew; second, instill a stern sense of duty; third, act with audacity.”* 

Historical doctrine, from the ancient Roman fleets to the fighting instructions of Admiral Hawke, teaches us that leadership at sea is a delicate trinitarian balance. 

First, there is absolute competence. A crew will forgive a commander many flaws, but they will never forgive ignorance of seamanship. The men must believe that the officer at the conn knows how to weather the storm that threatens to drown them. 

Second, there is justice tempered with humanity. The old doctrine of the lash and the iron fist is fading, and rightly so. Discipline maintained solely by fear breeds a quiet, simmering treason of the spirit. A true leader, as Collingwood so brilliantly demonstrated, governs by quiet authority. He must be as firm as oak when enforcing order, yet perceptive enough to know when a tired sailor needs an encouraging word rather than the brig. 

And finally, there is the quality of moral courage—the willingness to take the burden of decision entirely upon oneself. In the chaos of battle or the fury of a hurricane, committee has no place. The commander stands alone on the quarterdeck; his mind must be the calm center of the tempest.

I look at young Hawkins, with his literal mind and his awkward youth, and I realize my duty to him is not merely to teach him navigation or literary appreciation. It is to model that steady temper. If I can teach him to read the moods of the men as accurately as he reads the sky, he will do well enough when his own time comes to take the watch.

The bell has just struck eight. The watch is relieved. The timbers groan beneath me in their familiar, rhythmic song, and the Great Bear tilts slowly in the northern sky. I shall turn in, confident that the ship is in good hands, and the ocean will continue to roll on—whether Byron permits it or not.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poetic passage about being deep at sea that weaves together a reference to W.B. Yeats' poem "Sailing to Byzantium" and John Paul Jones' famous code of conduct for navy officers.
counterfactuals.output:
Far beyond the line where the sky drinks the wave, the mortal shore fades—for *that is no country for old men*, nor for the flesh that shivers in the wind. Out here in the vast, abyssal blue, the heart is unclasped from its *dying animal*, discarding its *tattered coat upon a stick* to yield to the ocean's cold *artifice of eternity*, where the starlit foam burns like *sages in God’s holy fire*.

Yet to ride these wild, unaging waters, *it is by no means enough to be merely a capable mariner*. Amidst the squall and the plunging dark, the officer upon the deck must become something more—the very soul of *patience, tact, and firmness*, bound by a *punctilious courtesy* toward the ruthless gales and holding fast to the *nicest sense of personal honor* when the world falls away into salt and silence.

Fastened to the wheel as the timbers groan, he stands erect against the void, guiding his wooden hull through the deep to sing to the endless night of *what is past, or passing, or to come*.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Impersonate an early 20th-century ship commander writing about life on the high seas. Describe the vast open water, an amusing moment trying to introduce high literature to your bosun mate, and conclude with your core philosophical beliefs about tact, justice, and evaluating mistakes in subordinates.
counterfactuals.output:
**12th October, 1911**  
**RMS *Caledonia*, at Sea**  
**Latitude 34° 12’ N, Longitude 42° 08’ W**

There is a terrifying purity to the deep ocean that no landsman can ever truly comprehend. For fourteen days, the horizon has remained a unbroken, hard-edged circle of sapphire and steel, binding us in a cathedral of salt and sky. The great steam turbines beneath my feet hum a ceaseless, rhythmic baritone, driving our steel hull through swells that were born off the coast of Greenland. At night, when the coal-smoke from our funnels drifts away into the dark, the sea ceases to be water; it becomes a vast mirror reflecting the icy, indifferent stars. Out here, stripped of the clamor of the ports, a man realizes how utterly insignificant his ambitions are, save for the timber and iron he stands upon and the duty he owes to the souls aboard.

Yet, life upon this blue desert is far from a somber affair, as human nature insists on asserting itself against the grand void. Only yesterday evening, I engaged in a brief experiment of cultural uplift which proved to be a magnificent failure. 

Having observed my Bosun’s Mate, Mr. Higgins—a man whose face resembles a weathered oak spar and whose vocabulary consists entirely of nautical jargon and colorful profanities—sitting idle on the foredeck, I felt a burst of misguided philanthropic zeal. I resolved to lend him my pocket volume of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. 

An hour later, I found him leaning against the capstan, staring at *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* with a look of profound, agonized suspicion, as though the book were a ticking naval mine.

“How do you find the verse, Higgins?” I inquired, pausing on my promenade.

Higgins removed his cap, scratched his grey head, and spat neatly into the lee scuppers. “Well, Captain, begging your pardon, but this Mariner chap is an absolute fool. Shootin’ an Albatross was poor form, aye, but his real crime was bad seamanship. If he’d paid attention to his glass instead of babbling about albatrosses and water-snakes, he’d have seen the gale coming and saved his crew the trouble of dying of thirst. And as for his ship being ‘as idle as a painted ship upon a painted ocean’—well, sir, if his hands had been turned out to scrub the decks and grease the blocks instead of whining, they’d have kept busy enough until the wind filled their canvas.”

I suppressed a smile, bade him keep the book, and retreated to the chartroom. It seems high literature is no match for thirty years of North Atlantic salt, and perhaps Mr. Higgins is the wiser man for it.

Yet, moments like these, warm with the foibles of men, remind me of the weight a Master carries. Command is not merely the calculation of coal consumption and nautical miles; it is the delicate art of governing men. Over my years on the bridge, I have forged a few quiet beliefs that serve as my compass.

First, as to **tact**: it is the oil that keeps the machinery of a ship running without friction. An officer who relies solely on the loud voice and the bark of authority is a poor officer indeed. Authority is a reserve of capital; if you spend it recklessly every hour, you will find yourself bankrupt when a real crisis strikes. Tact allows a commander to bend a man’s will without breaking his pride.

Second, as to **justice**: it must be as absolute and predictable as the tides, yet entirely free of personal malice. A crew will forgive a strict captain, even a hard one, provided his scales are balanced without favor. The moment a seaman suspects that discipline is meted out by temper rather than rule, the invisible threads of loyalty begin to fray.

Finally, in **evaluating the mistakes of subordinates**, a commander must possess a keen eye for motive. Mistakes of the head—born of ignorance, haste, or the sheer unpredictability of the sea—must be met with instruction and a firm, measured guidance. A man who never makes a mistake at sea is a man who never moves, and a ship needs movement. But mistakes of the heart—sloth, deceit, or the willful neglect of duty—must be struck down swiftly and without hesitation. The ocean is too swift to punish carelessness; a captain who tolerates a rot in his crew invites the sea to drown them all.

The glass is falling tonight, and the wind is beginning to sing in the rigging. I shall go above and check the watches. 

May God keep our course true, and our men steady.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of ocean fiction combining evocative, sensory prose about a ship plowing through deep water with a formal reflection on naval leadership and handling crew errors.
counterfactuals.output:
The *HMS Sovereign* cut through the ink-black expanse of the North Atlantic, her steel stem shearing the sea into twin plumes of phosphorescent white. Beneath the bridge wing, thirty-thousand tons of deadweight displacement thrummed with the deep, rhythmic stroke of steam turbines. The water here was abyssal, a crushing blackness rolling under a vault of low, bruised clouds. With every plunge into the trough, the hull groaned—a deep-chested, metallic sigh—before lifting again, driving through the obsidian surge with relentless, heavy purpose. The air was thick with the scent of ozone, cold brine, and hot engine oil blowing faint from the stacks.

Beside Captain Vance, the bridge was suspended in a tense, crimson-lit silence. Sub-Lieutenant Hayes stood paralyzed at the pelorus, his face pale beneath his oilskins. Moments earlier, Hayes had misjudged the onset of a beam sea, delaying the order to alter course. The resulting roll had taken the ship sixty feet down to her port rail, green water cascading over the forecastle, tearing away a deck locker and sending three sea-lashing crewmen tumbling into the scuppers. The danger had passed, but the air remained taut, charged with the horror of what a few degrees of hesitation might have wrought in the dark.

Vance did not yell. He gripped the salt-crusted brass rail, feeling the violence of the ocean transmit through the ship’s spine into his own palms. 

A sea command, he reflected, was ultimately an exercise in managing human fragility within an environment that permitted none. An officer’s authority did not derive from the execution of swift vengeance upon those who faltered, but from the deliberate, stoic absorption of shock. To react to a subordinate’s terror with anger was to compound the maritime danger with emotional chaos. 

Naval discipline demanded a rigorous taxonomy of error. Negligence and insolence were cancers to be cut out without hesitation; but the paralysis of youth, brought on by the sudden, suffocating realization of the ocean’s scale, required a different discipline altogether. A captain who shatters the spirit of a junior officer in the wake of a mistake deprives the vessel of a future commander. Conversely, one who glosses over the fault invites the sea to teach the lesson next time—and the sea was an indifferent teacher, prone to killing the pupil. The true art of command lay in holding the margin of error open just long enough for the mistake to become an indelible, life-giving scar.

The ship rose again, her bow rising high over a swell, spray lashing the thick quartz glass of the wheelhouse like thrown gravel. 

Vance turned slowly to Hayes. His voice, when he spoke, was low and unhurried, cutting cleanly through the roar of the wind and the deep churn of the screws.

"The ocean has just demonstrated the price of five seconds, Mr. Hayes," Vance said, his gaze steady on the young officer. "It is a cheap tuition, paid in paint and canvas rather than men. Correct our heading three degrees to starboard, steer into the wind, and hold the watch. You will not miss the swell again."

Hayes swallowed, the blood returning to his cheeks. He stood taller, his hand sweeping to the engine order telegraph with newfound precision. "Three degrees to starboard, sir. Aye."

Vance turned back to the dark water, watching the iron bow slice through the oncoming wave, burying itself in the deep, and rising once more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vignette about a naval officer far from land who turns to poetry and reflections on command to pass the time.
counterfactuals.output:
The Pacific at three in the morning was not romantic; it was a vast, indifferent engine. 

Commander Thomas Vance sat at the small brass-bound desk bolted to his cabin bulkhead. Outside the scuttle, the sea was black on black, a liquid night sliding endlessly past the steel hull of the frigate. Beneath his boots, the deep, rhythmic thrum of the twin shafts vibrated through the deckhead—a mechanical heartbeat that had not skipped in eleven days.

He uncapped his fountain pen. The blue-black ink pooled slightly on the crisp, unruled page of his notebook. 

Down in the messes, two hundred sailors slept, stacked three-high in the dark, dreaming of air-conditioned bedrooms, cold beers, and voices that didn't come through a static-laced intercom. On the bridge, six levels up, the Officer of the Deck stared into the green ghost-light of the radar, watching empty vectors. 

And here, in the quiet middle, sat Vance.

*Command,* he wrote, his handwriting small and tight, *is the art of being entirely surrounded yet entirely alone.*

He paused, watching a stray drop of sweat bead on his thumb. He wiped it on his trousers and leaned back, letting the gentle four-degree roll of the ship sway him against his chair. He turned to a fresh page, abandoning prose for something tighter, something that could hold the weight of the water outside.

> *The compass knows no mercy in its turn,*  
> *Nor does the tide care what the living burn.*  
> *We trace our lines upon a floor of slate,*  
> *And call the wind by names of rank and state.*  
> 
> *Two hundred heartbeats sleeping in the hull,*  
> *Beneath the gliding shadows of the gull.*  
> *I hold their morning softly in my hand,*  
> *A thousand leagues away from any land.*

He read the stanza back to himself in a whisper, testing the rhythm against the groaning of the ship's bulkheads. It was rough, but it served. Poetry, he had discovered three deployments ago, was the only thing capable of matching the compression of life at sea. A report was too rigid; a letter home was too guarded. But a line of verse could hold the silence of a middle watch without needing to explain it.

To his crew, Vance was the absolute authority—a calm, silver-haired figure in flame-resistant coveralls who signed off on tactical maneuvers, approved punishment, and decided when the ship turned into the wind. But command, he reflected, rubbing his tired eyes, was largely an exercise in restraint. It was the discipline of not speaking when a junior officer stumbled, of carrying the quiet panic of a faulty oil pressure valve alone so two hundred others could sleep through the night.

He tapped the pen against the paper. The ink left tiny, dark pinpricks on the page, like an archipelago of unmapped islands. 

Suddenly, the red telephone on his desk chimed—once, sharp and muted for the captain’s cabin.

Vance picked it up before the second ring.

"Captain," he said, his voice instantly clear, leaving no trace of the poet in the darkened room.

"Bridge, Officer of the Deck, sir," came the voice of Lieutenant Miller, crisp and precise. "Surface contact, bearing zero-eight-five, range twenty-two thousand yards. Course two-one-zero, speed twelve knots. Merchantman, by the radar profile."

"Very well, Mr. Miller," Vance replied softly. "Maintain track. Call me if the CPA drops below five thousand."

"Aye, sir. Goodnight, Captain."

"Goodnight, Miller."

Vance set the receiver back in its cradle. He looked down at the notebook. The ink was dry. He closed the leather cover, slipped the pen into his pocket, and stood up. He adjusted his coveralls, smoothed down his collar, and stepped toward the heavy steel door. 

The poems were for the dark, but the morning belonged to the ship.
